stem: What factor is the most important in deciding surgery for cleft palate?
srcNote: (Cleft lip) answer is confirmed when Q was reviewed with the course organiser. Choice D is blank in the source.
expl: Palate repair is planned for 12–18 months (before speech develops), but surgery is deep inside a small mouth — what decides that the child is ready is the mouth/palate examination (big enough for exposure and instruments). The source key is C.

why.A: Age is the guide (12–18 months), but it isn't absolute — some are repaired at ~10 months when the mouth allows.
why.B: Severity changes the operation, not the decision to operate — every cleft palate is repaired.

stem: What is the time of bone grafting for cleft palate?

opts.t: When the canine teeth come out

expl: The alveolar cleft is bone-grafted in mixed dentition, before the permanent canine erupts (~8–11 years), so the canine can erupt through the grafted bone and the arch is stabilized.

why.A: Speech timing is for palate repair (12–18 months).
why.C: Puberty is too late — the canine has already erupted.

stem: A 5-year-old child post-surgical fixation of his cleft of primary and secondary palate, went to rehabilitation center for speech therapy and assessment found to have nasal speech which is not responding well to palate exercises. What is the most likely contributing factor for his speech condition?

opts.t: Palatal fistula in the soft palate

expl: Persistent hypernasal speech after palate repair, not improved by exercises = velopharyngeal insufficiency — the soft palate can't close off the nasopharynx → speech assessment and possibly a secondary operation (pharyngoplasty).

why.A: Inadequate muscle repair can cause VPI, but VPI is the condition producing the speech.
why.C: The alveolus doesn't cause nasal speech.
why.D: A fistula can leak air but is usually in the hard palate and visible; persistent nasality after repair is VPI.

stem: A 4-month-old child with bilateral complete cleft of the primary palate with very short nasal columella and small prolabium. Weighs 5.5 kgs and has no other congenital anomalies. He was prepared for cleft surgery. Which of the following is the most difficult part of the surgical repair?
srcNote: Source key was A; corrected — see explanation. (Cleft lip)
expl: In a bilateral complete cleft lip, the very short columella and small prolabium make the nasal reconstruction (lengthening the columella, positioning the nasal tip and alar cartilages) the hardest part. The bony alveolus isn't repaired at 4 months — it is bone-grafted later, when the canines erupt. The source key was A.

why.A: The alveolar bone gap is grafted at ~8–11 years, not in the primary lip repair.
why.C: The sulcus is reconstructed but isn't the main difficulty.

stem: Which ONE of the following is the most common site for cleft palate?
srcNote: (Cleft lip) The source uses "cleft palate" in the stem and "Microfoam" in choice D. Both are preserved as written.
expl: Unilateral clefts are commoner than bilateral, and left-sided clefts are commoner than right (no clear reason is known).

why.D: (Microform clefts are the mildest form, not a site.)

stem: A mother with a baby with cleft palate presented to you complaining of a problem with feeding for the last 2 - 3 months and failure of gaining weight. Currently, his weight is 5Kg, what is the best choice for this concern to prepare the patient for surgery?
expl: A cleft baby failing to gain weight despite feeding problems needs his nutrition secured before surgery — feeding via a nasogastric tube while feeding technique is optimized. Weight and Hb (Rule of 10s) show readiness for surgery.

why.B: The problem is mechanical feeding, not a primary medical illness.
why.D: Changing formula doesn't fix the poor seal.

stem: At which gestational age is the development of the primary palate?
srcNote: Source key was B; corrected — see explanation. (Cleft lip) ( in the tutorial notes it is written at 15 wk, the closest choice is C) The source answer B conflicts with its own tutorial-note comment suggesting C.
expl: The lip and primary palate (premaxilla) form at about 4–7 weeks; the secondary palate fuses at 8–12 weeks. The source key (8–12 weeks) is the timing of the secondary palate.

why.C: Palate formation is complete by then.
why.D: The palate is formed well before birth.
